newsitem.title: USA: Albright sets new style with Houston trip.
newsitem.headline: Albright sets new style with Houston trip.

text.p: Madeleine Albright carved out a new style as secretary of state on Friday, paying a high-profile, campaign-style visit to Texas even before embarking on her first overseas trip.

Her aim is to bring to an increasingly inward-looking American people the message that foreign policy matters -- and, by implication, that the State Department is justified in its bid for an increase in its hitherto declining budget.
As part of her two-day trip she scheduled appointments with former President George Bush and former Secretary of State James Baker, both Texans and both Republicans.

Aides said she was underscoring the new bipartisan approach of the Democratic Clinton administration, especially to gain support for its bid to make Congress ratify the Chemical Weapons Convention, which Bush and Baker both favour.

The centerpieces of her visit were a meeting with Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria, whom she invited to this oil city in Texas, which shares a long border with Mexico, and a foreign policy speech at Houston's Rice University.
But in between she found time to visit a U.S. passport office and a high school in Houston. In both places she was applauded and cheered.

It was Albright's predecessor, the low-profile Warren Christopher, who launched a State Department bid to promote itself through "town meetings" around the country. But Christopher seldom took part in these himself, sending aides.
Albright, America's first woman secretary of state, "wants to be visible and she wants to raise morale (in the State Department)," said spokesman Nicholas Burns. "It's a difference of style."
"She wanted to get out and see the country, which is why she's going to Houston before she goes overseas," Burns added.

Big bucks are at stake. A continuous fall in America's foreign spending is blamed by officials on growing indifference to events abroad among a public that does not understand what the State Department does or why it matters.

This week, the Clinton administration sought to reverse that trend, submitting a budget that called for a seven percent funding increase. Albright's charm and charisma are seen as an important weapon in obtaining that hike.
Albright swept through a regional passport office run by State Department employees in downtown Houston, talking to applicants standing in line at the windows.

When one Chinese-American said he needed a passport to visit the land of his ancestors, she told him: "I'm going to China, too." Later, she sat down at a computer in a back office and issued a passport for another applicant.

At the city's Lamar High School, she gestured at a map of the world pinned to the wall to illustrate a round-the-world tour she will start on Feb. 15, and confided to students: "I failed geography when I was five years old."

Insisting that she had since improved her geography, she explained that unlike previous secretaries of state, whose first tours were just to Europe, she was visiting Asia as well because it was "equally important."
Besides, she said, "I figure I've got to do something different from other people."
